newsitem.title: ITALY: IMF says Italy must do more to win EMU berth.
newsitem.headline: IMF says Italy must do more to win EMU berth.

text.p: Membership of the single European currency is within Italy's reach provided that the government cracks down on state spending, the International Monetary Fund said in a report published on Monday.

The Washington-based group said Prime Minister Romano Prodi had embarked on a bold bid to book Italy a place in European economic and monetary union (EMU) but warned that the price of missing the boat would be high.

"We would note that the government's decision that Italy should strive to join EMU from the start has substantially raised the stakes, amplifying not only the payoffs for success but also the penalties for failure," the IMF said.

The government has prepared a massive 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) deficit-cutting budget for next year to meet tough guidelines laid out for countries wishing to join EMU from its launch in 1999.
While welcoming the austerity package, which includes hefty tax rises but leaves welfare spending unscathed, the IMF said it did not think it would be enough to guarantee EMU membership.

"We call for the definition, as early as possible in 1997, of durable cost-saving measures affecting spending on social security, health and public employment," said the report, which was written after a recent visit to Italy by IMF experts.
The IMF predicted that the 1996 public sector deficit would yawn to 133 trillion lire -- 7.1 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- against an original 109.4 trillion lire target.
Prodi has promised to bring the deficit/GDP ratio down to 3.1 percent next year compared to the three percent level established in the Maastricht Treaty for EMU aspirants.

The IMF forecast a ratio of around 3.75 percent in 1997 but added that, if structural measures were introduced by early next year, Italy could maintain a budget deficit of just under three percent of GDP in 1998 and beyond.
"With resolute leadership and early action...success is within Italy's grasp," the IMF said.

To achieve this, the report urged Prodi to speed up pension reform and called for the strict enforcement of a hiring freeze in the state sector. But it said spending cuts alone might not achieve all the savings needed to secure 1997 financial goals.
"Any action on the revenue side should, however, firmly avoid further increases in an already excessive burden of direction taxation," it cautioned.
If the government could not muster the political will to push through a further packet of tough budget medicine, then it should concentrate on achieving the EU Maastricht criteria in 1998.
"This confirms that Italy's ambitions to be in at the start of monetary union is not just credible but also within reach," he told reporters.

However, the IMF warned of dire consequences if market hopes that EMU membership was around the corner proved false. It noted that market rates had fallen sharply in recent months as investors bet that Italy would win its EMU battle.

"But to the extent that they reflect "convergence plays' by market participants, they run the risk of unravelling... Any such development in 1997-98 would prove extremely costly," the IMF said. $1 = 1,524 lire
